text: I honestly think having my phone on me all the time wrecks my ability to focus deep on anything. The constant influx of notifications, alerts, and digital interruptions fragments attention and impairs the cognitive processes associated with sustained, focused engagement on a single task. Empirical research further indicates that the mere presence of a smartphone, even when powered off, can reduce available cognitive capacity and degrade performance on attention-demanding activities. Like, even when its facedown I still feel that pull to check it. A real example: last week I sat down to write a lab report and figured it would take maybe an hour. But every few minutes I grabbed my phone for a Snap or to scroll TikTok for "just a sec," and that hour turned into almost three. This phenomenon is consistent with the concept of attention residue, wherein the act of switching between tasks leaves a portion of one's cognitive resources lingering on the previous activity, thereby diminishing the quality and efficiency of performance on the subsequent task. By the end I couldnt even remember what point I was trying to make in the intro. So yeah, I'd argue the always-on connectivity definitely harms focus way more than it helps. Cultivating periods of intentional disconnection has been shown to facilitate deeper concentration and to support the kind of uninterrupted cognitive immersion that complex intellectual work requires. When I leave my phone in another room I get like twice as much done, no joke.
